propositions.text: The Applicant seeks judicial review of the RAD decision confirming the RPD's determination that he is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Abdulaziz Ziyad Kider, seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (“RAD”) dated October 28, 2020, confirming the determination of the Refugee Protection Division (“RPD") that the Applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (“IRPA”).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant seeks judicial review of the RAD decision confirming the RPD's negative refugee determination.

propositions.text: The Applicant fears persecution in Ethiopia due to political views, ethnicity, and father's activities; RAD dismissed claim for lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The Applicant fears persecution in Ethiopia because of his anti-government political views, his Gurage ethnicity, and his father’s anti-government activities. The RAD dismissed the Applicant’s claim because it found allegations central to the Applicant’s claim were not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant fears persecution for political views, ethnicity, and father's activities; RAD dismissed claim for credibility reasons.

propositions.text: The RAD failed to observe natural justice by not allowing submissions on facts found not credibly established by RAD but undisputed by RPD.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the RAD failed to observe the principles of natural justice by not giving the Applicant an opportunity to make submissions and present evidence on facts which were not disputed by the RPD, but which the RAD found to be not credibly established.

propositions.text: The RAD erred in determining central allegations and in its credibility findings.
propositions.quote: The Applicant further submits that the RAD erred in its determination of the central allegations in the Applicant’s claim, and erred in its credibility findings.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues RAD breached natural justice by denying submissions on undisputed facts and erred in central allegations and credibility findings.

propositions.text: The RAD breached procedural fairness by not allowing submissions on findings beyond RPD's; judicial review is allowed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I find the RAD breached its duty of procedural fairness by failing to give the Applicant the opportunity to make further submissions on findings of fact that went beyond the findings of the RPD. I therefore allow this application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD breached procedural fairness by denying submissions on findings beyond RPD's and allows judicial review.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a 22-year-old Ethiopian citizen of Gurage ethnicity.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 22-year-old citizen of Ethiopia of Gurage ethnicity.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a 22-year-old Ethiopian citizen of Gurage ethnicity.

propositions.text: Applicant participated in protests in 2016 and 2017 at Mekelle University and left university in 2018 due to ethnic tensions and harassment.
propositions.quote: The Applicant claims that he participated in protests in August 2016 and December 2017, while studying at Mekelle University, but managed to avoid the mass arrests that took place. The Applicant states that he left university in June 2018 because of ethnic tensions, particularly because non-Tigrean students such as himself faced harassment and discrimination from Tigrean students.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant participated in protests and left university due to ethnic tensions and harassment.

propositions.text: In summer 2018, Applicant and father visited Welkite where TPLF attacked Gurage; Applicant detained July 2-7, 2018, released with warning.
propositions.quote: In the summer of 2018, the Applicant and his father visited family in Welkite, where the Tigray People’s Liberation Front attacked people belonging to the Gurage ethnic group. The Applicant states that he was among those who tried to defend the Gurage from looting and property damages. Because of his participation in this event, the Applicant was arrested and detained in a military camp from July 2-7, 2018. He was released with a warning not to participate in any future protests.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant was detained in July 2018 after defending Gurage in Welkite and released with a warning.

propositions.text: Applicant's father detained six weeks in 2005 for political protests and later harassed for opposition support.
propositions.quote: The Applicant also claims that his father was detained for six weeks in November 2005 for his participation in political protests, and was later targeted and harassed for his perceived identity as a supporter of an outlawed opposition party.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant's father was detained in 2005 for protests and later harassed for opposition support.

propositions.text: Applicant came to Canada on student visa in late 2018 and claimed refugee status based on political opinion, ethnicity, and father's activities.
propositions.quote: The Applicant came to Canada on a student visa in late 2018. Once in Canada, he made a refugee claim on the basis that he fears persecution due to his political opinion, ethnicity, as well as his father’s anti-government activities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Applicant came to Canada in 2018 and claimed refugee status based on political opinion, ethnicity, and father's activities.

propositions.text: On January 2, 2020, RPD determined Applicant was not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection; credibility was key issue.
propositions.quote: On January 2, 2020, the RPD determined that the Applicant was not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. The determinative issue for the RPD was credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD decided on January 2, 2020, that Applicant was not a refugee or protected person, with credibility as key issue.

propositions.text: RPD doubted all Applicant's allegations due to credibility concerns and lack of credible evidence he is wanted by Ethiopian authorities.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that credibility concerns which were central to the Applicant’s claim led the RPD “to doubt the veracity of all the claimant’s allegations,” finding that the Applicant had not provided sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence to establish the allegations that he is wanted by Ethiopian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility concerns led it to doubt all Applicant's allegations and lack credible evidence he is wanted by authorities.

propositions.text: RPD found discrepancies between Applicant's testimony and BOC, including father's detention omission, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a negative inference with respect to the Applicant’s overall credibility because of discrepancies between the Applicant’s testimony and his Basis of Claim (“BOC”). For instance, at the RPD hearing, the Applicant stated that his father was detained with him from July 2-7, 2018, yet this was not mentioned in his BOC. The RPD was not satisfied with the Applicant’s reasons for not mentioning his father in the BOC, and found this omission to be a significant element of his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found discrepancies between Applicant's testimony and BOC, including omission of father's detention, harming credibility.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicant was not beaten and not wanted by Ethiopian authorities on balance of probabilities due to inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: Based on the inconsistencies between the Applicant’s BOC and his testimony, the RPD found that the Applicant had not been beaten by the police or anyone else in Ethiopia, and that, on a balance of probabilities, the Applicant was not wanted by Ethiopian authorities following his arrest in July 2018, nor would he be in the future if he were to return to Ethiopia.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Applicant was not beaten and not wanted by authorities on balance of probabilities due to inconsistencies.

propositions.text: RPD accepted Applicant's participation in 2016 protest and July 2018 detention but gave little weight to friend's statement about being wanted by authorities.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s claim included a statement from his friend confirming his presence at the August 16, 2016 protest, and a letter from his great-uncle confirming that the Applicant was involved in the protest in Welkite in 2018. The RPD did not dispute that the Applicant participated in the August 16, 2016 protest and accepted that he was detained in July 2018. However, since the Applicant was not arrested or detained until two years later in July 2018, the RPD assigned little weight to the friend’s statement to establish that the Applicant is wanted by Ethiopian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD accepted Applicant's protest participation and detention but gave little weight to friend's statement about being wanted by authorities.

propositions.text: Applicant appealed RPD decision to RAD without providing new evidence.
propositions.quote: The Applicant appealed the RPD decision to the RAD. No new evidence was provided to support the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD decision was appealed to RAD without new evidence.

propositions.text: On October 28, 2020, RAD dismissed appeal, confirmed RPD decision, citing credibility issues and inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: On October 28, 2020, the RAD dismissed the Applicant’s appeal and confirmed the RPD’s decision. The determinative ground for the dismissal of the appeal was credibility. The RAD found that there were numerous omissions and inconsistencies between the Applicant’s BOC and his testimony at the RPD hearing. The RAD also doubted the veracity of the Applicant’s allegations and agreed with the RPD that the Applicant is not, on balance of probabilities, wanted by Ethiopian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismissed the appeal, confirmed RPD decision, citing credibility issues and inconsistencies.

propositions.text: RAD independently found all central allegations untrue on balance of probabilities and insufficient credible evidence of persecution risk.
propositions.quote: The RAD concludes, in its independent analysis and unlike the RPD, that all of the central allegations in the appellant’s case, including his alleged participation in the August 2016 protest and his July 2018 arrest and detention, are not true, on a balance of probabilities. The RAD therefore finds that it has insufficient credible evidence upon which to find that the appellant is similarly situated to any persecuted person in Ethiopia.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD independently found all central allegations untrue and insufficient credible evidence of persecution risk.

propositions.text: RAD gave no weight to great-uncle's letter due to unexplained omission of father's arrest, discrediting the letter.
propositions.quote: In its independent analysis, however, the RAD finds that the unreasonably explained omission of his father’s alleged arrest and detention is sufficient to discredit the letter entirely.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD discredited the great-uncle's letter due to unexplained omission of father's arrest.

propositions.text: Applicant submits issues: RAD's unfair procedure, erroneous central allegation finding, uncontradicted evidence, and credibility assessment error.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that this application for judicial review raises the following issues: Whether the RAD followed unfair procedure in arriving at the impugned decision; Whether the RAD’s finding about the central allegation in the claim was erroneous; Whether the uncontradicted evidence establishes the Applicant’s claim; and Whether the panel erred in assessing the credibility of the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant submits issues of RAD's unfair procedure, erroneous findings, uncontradicted evidence, and credibility errors.

propositions.text: Court frames issues as whether RAD breached procedural fairness and whether RAD's decision is reasonable.
propositions.quote: I see the issues in this case as follows: Whether the RAD breached procedural fairness. Whether the RAD’s decision is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames issues as RAD's procedural fairness breach and decision reasonableness.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the RAD decision is reasonable, with reasonableness as the standard of review.
propositions.quote: The Respondent states that the issue is whether the decision of the RAD is reasonable and submits that the applicable standard of review is reasonableness.

propositions.text: Applicant frames issue as fairness, but argument relates to adequacy of reasons, a substantive review matter.
propositions.quote: while the Applicant frames the issue as one of fairness, the substance of their argument relates to the adequacy of the reasons – which is properly considered under substantive review.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says issue is reasonableness of RAD decision and Applicant's fairness argument is about adequacy of reasons, a substantive review matter.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness issue should be reviewed on correctness standard; other issues on reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the issue of procedural fairness ought to be reviewed on the standard of correctness, and that the remaining issue ought to be reviewed on the standard of reasonableness.

propositions.text: Agrees procedural fairness is correctness standard; other issues reasonableness standard, citing Vavilov.
propositions.quote: I agree: the first issue is to be reviewed on the standard of correctness, and the second on the standard of reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 (“Vavilov”) at paras 10, 16-17).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says procedural fairness is correctness standard; court agrees, citing Vavilov, with other issues reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is deferential but robust; decision must be transparent, intelligible, justified.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness is a deferential, but robust, standard of review (Vavilov at paras 12-13). The reviewing court must determine whether the decision under review, including both its rationale and outcome, is transparent, intelligible and justified (Vavilov at para 15).

propositions.text: Reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, justified by facts and law.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker (Vavilov at para 85).

propositions.text: Reasonableness depends on administrative context, record, and impact on affected persons.
propositions.quote: Whether a decision is reasonable depends on the relevant administrative setting, the record before the decision-maker, and the impact of the decision on those affected by its consequences (Vavilov at paras 88-90, 94, 133-135).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains reasonableness standard as deferential, requiring transparency, coherence, justification, and context consideration, citing Vavilov.

propositions.text: To find unreasonableness, flaws must be central or significant.
propositions.quote: For a decision to be unreasonable, an applicant must establish the decision contains flaws that are sufficiently central or significant (Vavilov at para 100).

propositions.text: Court must not reweigh evidence or interfere with factual findings absent exceptional circumstances.
propositions.quote: A reviewing court must refrain from reweighing the evidence that was before the decision-maker, and it should not interfere with factual findings absent exceptional circumstances (Vavilov at para 125).

paragraphs.summary: Court states unreasonableness requires central flaws; court must not reweigh evidence or disturb factual findings except in exceptional cases.

propositions.text: Correctness is non-deferential; procedural fairness asks if procedure was fair considering all circumstances and Baker factors.
propositions.quote: Correctness, in contrast, is a non-deferential standard of review. The central question for issues of procedural fairness is whether the procedure was fair, having regard to all of the circumstances, including the factors enumerated in Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paragraphs 21-28 (Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains correctness standard is non-deferential and applies to procedural fairness, considering all circumstances and Baker factors.

propositions.text: RPD made negative credibility inferences but accepted protest participation and detention occurred.
propositions.quote: While the RPD made negative credibility inferences with respect to certain aspects of the Applicant’s participation in the August 2016 protest and the Applicant’s detention in July 2018, it nonetheless accepted that these incidents occurred.

propositions.text: RAD independently found all central allegations, including protest and detention, were not true on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The RAD, however, conducted an independent analysis and found that, on a balance of probabilities, “all the central allegations in this case, including the appellant’s alleged participation in the August 2016 protest and his alleged arrest and detention in July 2018, are not true.”

paragraphs.summary: RPD accepted protest and detention occurred despite credibility doubts; RAD independently found these central allegations untrue.

propositions.text: RAD should have given reasonable opportunity to respond to facts rejected by RAD but accepted by RPD.
propositions.quote: The Applicant concedes that his credibility was questioned by the RPD, yet he submits that the RAD should have provided him with a reasonable opportunity to make submissions with respect to the facts, which were rejected by the RAD, yet accepted by the RPD.

propositions.text: Participation in protest and detention were not live issues before RAD; RAD erred by raising them without notice.
propositions.quote: The Applicant contends that the fact that he participated in the August 2016 protest and was detained in July 2018 were not live issues in the appeal before the RAD, and that the RAD committed a reviewable error by raising these issues in the appeal and failing to give him notice that the issues would be raised.

propositions.text: Unreasonable to expect submissions on appeal about facts accepted by RPD and not in dispute.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that it is unreasonable to expect him to make submissions on appeal regarding issues and facts that were accepted by the RPD and thus not in dispute.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD erred by raising protest and detention issues without notice and should have allowed submissions on facts accepted by RPD.

propositions.text: RAD's negative factual finding based on same credibility issues identified by RPD, no new credibility matters.
propositions.quote: While the RAD’s independent assessment of the appellant’s claim has arrived at a negative factual finding that is more extensive than the alleged facts rejected by the RPD, the RAD has arrived at that finding based on the same particular credibility issues that were identified and discussed by the RPD in its decision, and not based on any new credibility matters that the RAD perceived in the record that were not identified and relied upon by the RPD in arriving at its negative credibility conclusion.

propositions.text: RAD satisfied appellant had notice of issues motivating its decision.
propositions.quote: The RAD is therefore satisfied that the appellant has had notice of the issues motivating the RAD’s decision.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found negative facts based on same credibility issues as RPD and was satisfied appellant had notice of issues motivating its decision.

propositions.text: RAD lacks jurisdiction to consider issues not relied on by RPD and not subject of appeal.
propositions.quote: the RAD does not possess the jurisdiction to consider an issue that, although fully canvassed before the RPD, was not relied upon in its decision and therefore was not the subject matter of the Applicant’s appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD lacks jurisdiction to consider issues not relied on by RPD and not appealed.

propositions.text: RPD denied claim based on not being wanted by Ethiopian authorities; Applicant's appeal focused on this accepted fact.
propositions.quote: The Applicant states that the RPD denied his claim based on the determination that he is not wanted by Ethiopian authorities. The Applicant submits that although he addressed the RPD’s credibility concerns in his appeal, the crux of his argument was based on the issue that led to the denial of his claim – notably the Ethiopian authorities’ continued interest in him and the possibility of being persecuted.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD erred by relying on issues considered but not relied on by RPD, citing Ojarikre.
propositions.quote: As in the case of Ojarikre, the Applicant argues that the RAD erred by relying on an issue which was considered, but not relied on by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says RPD denied claim on accepted facts; RAD erred by relying on issues not relied on by RPD, citing Ojarikre.

propositions.text: Cites Ching applying Mian: appellate courts raising new issues must notify parties and allow response.
propositions.quote: The Applicant also relies on this Court’s decision in Ching v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 725 (“Ching”), which applies the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision in R v Mian, 2014 SCC 54 (“Mian”) with regards to the scope of an appellate court’s jurisdiction to raise new issues.

propositions.text: Mian principles apply beyond criminal appeals; RAD must notify and allow submissions on new issues to avoid injustice.
propositions.quote: In my view, these principles should apply beyond the context of criminal appeals and, with the necessary modifications, to the context of appeals before the RAD. The RAD should first consider if the issue is “new” and if failing to raise the new issue would risk injustice. If the RAD pursues the new issue, it seems clear that procedural fairness requires that the party or parties affected be given notice and an opportunity to make submissions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant relies on Ching and Mian that RAD must notify and allow submissions on new issues to avoid injustice.

propositions.text: RAD's fact finding was procedurally unfair and tainted rest of decision.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the rest of the RAD’s decision is coloured by its fact finding, which was itself procedurally unfair.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits RAD's fact finding was procedurally unfair and tainted the decision.

propositions.text: No procedural fairness issue arises; new factual findings were minor and did not require notice.
propositions.quote: The Respondent contends that a procedural fairness issue does not arise in this case, and that while the RAD did make new findings on some minor factual points, those new findings of fact did not require notice to the Applicant because they were not determinative and they formed part of the RAD’s independent assessment.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues no procedural fairness issue; RAD's new factual findings were minor and did not require notice.

propositions.text: RAD and RPD agreed on core findings: no credible risk of persecution, not wanted by police, no assault.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the RAD agreed with the RPD on the core, determinative findings: both tribunals found that the Applicant did not credibly establish that he faces a risk of persecution in Ethiopia; both tribunals determined that the Applicant is not wanted by the police, nor was he ever assaulted by the police, as reflected in his testimony; and both tribunals found that these admissions undermine the core of the Applicant’s refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says RAD and RPD agreed on core findings undermining Applicant's refugee claim.

propositions.text: RAD not bound by RPD's fact findings and may conduct independent assessment.
propositions.quote: The Respondent states that this Court has noted that the RAD is not required to show deference to the RPD’s finding of fact, and is entitled to conduct an independent assessment of the record before the RPD when addressing issues raised by the parties (Tan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 876 (“Tan”), at para 40).

propositions.text: Parties should respond to new issues; RAD generally cannot raise issues not raised by parties or RPD.
propositions.quote: In Tan, this Court found that a party should have an opportunity to respond to new issues and concerns that will have a bearing on a decision impacting them and it is generally not open to the RAD to raise an issue that was not raised by the parties or the RPD (Tan at para 32).

propositions.text: Different view of evidence by RAD from RPD is not a fairness ground if no new issue raised.
propositions.quote: The fact that the RAD views some of the evidence differently from the RPD is not a basis to challenge the RPD’s decision on fairness grounds when no new issue has been raised (Tan at para 40).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent cites Tan: RAD may independently assess facts but cannot raise new issues without notice; differing views not fairness grounds.

propositions.text: Applicant had duty to respond to RPD credibility findings on appeal per RAD rules.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that given the findings of the RPD, the Applicant had a duty to respond to the credibility determination on appeal.

propositions.text: RAD Rules require full, detailed submissions on errors forming grounds of appeal.
propositions.quote: Rule 3(3)(g) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules, SOR/2012-257 states that an applicant must provide full and detailed submissions regarding the errors forming the grounds for appeal, and identify where those errors are found in the RPD’s decision.

propositions.text: RAD must focus on errors alleged by applicant and not consider arguments not raised by applicant.
propositions.quote: The RAD must focus on the specific errors the applicant alleges were made by the RPD (Dahal v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) 2017 FC 1102 at para 30), and “cannot be faulted on judicial review for not having considered or addressed arguments not raised [by the applicant]” (Cruz v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 22, at para 30).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Applicant had duty to respond to RPD credibility findings and RAD must focus on alleged errors only.

propositions.text: RPD doubted all aspects of claim; Applicant should have been on notice to respond on appeal.
propositions.quote: The Respondent further states that the RPD was clear in its assessment that it doubted the veracity of all aspects of the Applicant’s claim and that the Applicant should have thus already been “put on notice” that he would have to respond to these credibility findings on appeal to the RAD.

propositions.text: Applicant's failure to provide new evidence or submissions on appeal was at his own peril.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Applicant’s failure to provide new evidence to support his appeal or make new submissions to address the credibility issues was done at his own peril (Ghauri v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 548 at para 34).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says RPD doubted claim's veracity; Applicant should have responded on appeal and failed at own peril.

propositions.text: RAD's new findings were not minor and required notice to Applicant.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with the Respondent that the RAD’s new findings were only minor factual points that did not require notice to the Applicant.

propositions.text: Participation in protest and detention are central elements of Applicant's claim and arguments before RAD.
propositions.quote: Since the thrust of the Applicant’s arguments before the RAD involved his fear of persecution in Ethiopia and whether the authorities were interested in him, I find that his participation in the August 2016 protest and his detention in July 2018 are central elements of the Applicant’s claim.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD's new findings were not minor and that protest participation and detention are central to Applicant's claim.

propositions.text: In Abiodun, RAD breached fairness by making adverse credibility findings without giving chance to respond.
propositions.quote: In Abiodun v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 642, this Court found that the RAD breached procedural fairness when it concluded that the applicants were not credible based on alleged inconsistencies between their testimony and BOC narrative without putting those inconsistencies to the applicants for a chance to respond.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Abiodun where RAD breached fairness by making adverse credibility findings without notice to respond.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requires RAD to give notice that RPD's factual findings are live issues on appeal.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant’s submission that procedural fairness requires the RAD to give an applicant notice that the RPD’s findings of fact are a live issue in their appeal.

propositions.text: Disagrees with Respondent that Applicant was on notice to address all credibility aspects on appeal.
propositions.quote: I disagree with the Respondent’s reasoning that the Applicant was put on notice that he would need to address the credibility of all aspects of his claim on appeal to the RAD.

propositions.text: Applicant's appeal relied on RPD's acceptance of protest participation and detention; appeal focused on fear of persecution, not accepted facts.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s appeal to the RAD relied on the RPD’s finding that it was undisputed that he participated in the protest in August 2016 and was detained in July 2018. The Applicant’s appeal thus focused on the issue of whether there was a well-founded fear of persecution in Ethiopia, not on facts that were accepted by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: Court holds procedural fairness requires notice of live factual issues; Applicant was not on notice to address all credibility aspects; appeal focused on fear of persecution.

propositions.text: The RAD's decision as a whole cannot stand due to a breach of fairness.
propositions.quote: I find that the RAD’s decision as a whole cannot stand.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's decision cannot stand due to a breach of fairness.

propositions.text: It is unnecessary to address the reasonableness arguments but the RAD's decision is unreasonable for other reasons.
propositions.quote: While it is unnecessary to address the Applicant’s arguments with respect to the reasonableness of the decision under review, I find that there are issues with the RAD’s decision that also render it unreasonable.

propositions.text: The RAD initially identified the Applicant's fear of persecution due to opposition, ethnicity, and father's political activities.
propositions.quote: the RAD initially identified that the Applicant allegedly fears persecution at the hands of the Ethiopian government because of his opposition to the Ethiopian regime, his Gurage ethnicity, and his father’s political activities

propositions.text: The RAD failed to consider the Applicant's claim in its entirety.
propositions.quote: the RAD failed to consider the Applicant’s claim in its entirety.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's decision unreasonable for failing to consider the Applicant's full claim despite initially identifying key persecution grounds.

propositions.text: The RAD failed to meaningfully address evidence about ethnicity, political opinion, and father's political profile.
propositions.quote: The RAD failed to meaningfully address the Applicant’s evidence concerning his Gurage ethnicity, political opinion, or his father’s political profile

propositions.text: The RAD failed to consider how Ethiopia treats individuals with the Applicant's profile.
propositions.quote: and how the government of Ethiopia has treated individuals with the same profile as the Applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel argued the Court must speculate if the RAD would have decided differently if other persecution grounds were considered.
propositions.quote: As it was rightly noted by the Applicant’s counsel during the hearing, this leaves the Court to speculate whether the RAD would have arrived at a different conclusion had they considered the other grounds of persecution raised by the Applicant on appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD failed to address key evidence and notes the Applicant's counsel argued the Court must speculate on the RAD's decision if all grounds were considered.

propositions.text: The RAD breached procedural fairness by exceeding the RPD's factual findings and denying the Applicant further submissions.
propositions.quote: I find that the RAD breached its duty of procedural fairness by going beyond the RPD’s finding of facts and failing to provide the Applicant the opportunity to make further submissions.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is allowed.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD breached procedural fairness and allows the judicial review application.

propositions.text: No questions for certification were raised and none arise.
propositions.quote: No questions for certification were raised, and I agree that none arise.

propositions.text: The judicial review is allowed, the decision is set aside, and the matter is referred back to a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is allowed.The decision under review is set aside and the matter is referred back for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no certification questions and orders the judicial review allowed, decision set aside, and matter referred back.
